title: Terminally Online
blurb: Five words that only mean what they mean because of the internet.

words.note: Originally a heavy blow — a clout round the ear. It meant force long before it meant followers, which is either a downgrade or exactly the same thing.
We borrowed the word from epidemiology and kept the metaphor intact: something small, self-replicating, and not obviously good for you.

words.definition: Someone provoking a reaction for sport.
words.note: Not the bridge-dwelling monster. It comes from trolling, the fishing technique — dragging bait slowly behind a boat to see what bites.

words.definition: Admirably indifferent to what anyone thinks.
words.note: Coined by rapper Lil B, who took it back from an insult and made it a compliment. One of the few slang terms with a documented author.

words.definition: More replies than likes. A public verdict.
words.note: A cold mathematical term repurposed as one of the internet's cruellest judgements. Nobody announces their own ratio.

title: Red Flags
blurb: Things your friends noticed before you did.

words.note: From the Greek toxikon, the poison Greek archers smeared on arrows. The word has always been about something aimed at you.

words.definition: To vanish rather than have the conversation.
words.note: The verb only dates to the 2010s, but it is a very old idea with a new name: the person is still there, just no longer visible to you.
From the French petit, small. It meant literally minor before it meant deliberately so — the modern sense is almost a boast.

words.definition: Bitter about losing and showing it.
words.note: Likely from sailors, whose language and temperament were both described as salty long before anyone was salty in a group chat.

words.definition: Not quite honest, and not quite deniable.
words.note: Shade as an insult comes from Black and Latino ballroom culture, where throwing shade was an art form: the insult you could not quite prove.

title: Big Feelings
blurb: Precise names for things you have felt but not labelled.

words.note: Shares a root with merry. It is specifically the sociable kind of joy — you can be happy alone, but mirth wants company.

words.definition: Fear of something not here yet.
words.note: The useful distinction: fear points at something present, dread points at the future. Dread is the more exhausting of the two.

words.definition: A small doubt that arrives uninvited.
words.note: Originally meant a sudden wave of sickness or faintness. The modern sense kept the physical suddenness and moved it into the conscience.

words.definition: Burning enthusiasm, usually for a person.
words.note: From the Latin ardere, to burn — the same root as arson. English kept the heat and dropped the damage.
Taken whole from German, via Freud and Kierkegaard. English had no word for anxiety-about-nothing-specific, which is a strange gap for English to have had.

title: Money Moves
blurb: Five ways value changes hands, not all of them legal.

words.definition: A long con dressed as a business.
words.note: American carnival slang from around 1900. It implies patience — a grift is worked, not pulled.

words.definition: To accumulate well past the point of use.
words.note: Not the same as a horde, which is a crowd. One is treasure, the other is people, and they are unrelated words that sound identical.

words.definition: Anything you own that counts for something.
words.note: From the Anglo-French aver assetz, to have enough. The singular asset was reverse-engineered from assets, which came first.
Originally a piece of bread given to a beggar. It drifted from charity to theft to corruption in about three hundred years.

words.definition: A tenth, given whether you want to or not.
words.note: Literally the old English word for tenth. The number is baked into the word, which is why a nine percent tithe is a contradiction.

title: Doomscroll
blurb: It is 1am and you are still going.

words.definition: Consuming far more than intended, in one sitting.
words.note: A Lincolnshire dialect word meaning to soak a wooden vessel until it stopped leaking. The drinking sense came first; the television sense is very recent.
Lurker is one of the oldest pieces of internet slang, in use on Usenet by the early 1980s and essentially unchanged since.

words.definition: Short videos; also what your head does after.
words.note: A genuine double meaning: reel is film wound on a spool, and to reel is to stagger. Both apply.
The theft sense is nineteenth-century slang. That we now use the same gesture-word to dismiss people is a coincidence worth sitting with.

words.definition: A short puff of praise on a cover.
words.note: Invented in 1907 by humorist Gelett Burgess, who put a fictional Miss Belinda Blurb on a book jacket as a joke. The joke became the industry standard.

title: Worth Knowing
blurb: The quiet ones. You will use at least two of these.

words.note: Also a verb for easing a conscience — you salve your guilt. The physical and moral senses have run in parallel for a thousand years.
From the Arabic nazir, opposite — it is the astronomical point directly beneath you, exactly opposite the zenith. Arabic gave English most of its star vocabulary.

words.definition: The character of a group, as lived rather than stated.
words.note: One of Aristotle's three means of persuasion, alongside pathos and logos. Ethos is the argument that you are worth listening to.

words.definition: A small trained core inside a larger body.
words.note: From the French for frame — the cadre is the frame a larger organisation is built onto. Same root as cadre in painting: the thing around the picture.
From the Latin tacere, to be silent — the same root as taciturn. A tacit agreement is binding precisely because nobody wrote it down.

title: Heartbreak
blurb: Five words for one bad week.

words.note: Originally meant to kick. The physical sense survives in the word's tone — to be spurned is worse than to be refused.
Originally a hunting term: the appointed place where you waited for the game to be driven towards you. Make of that what you will.

words.definition: What is still warm after the fire.
words.note: An unusually old word, barely changed from Old English aemerge. It has always meant the part that outlasts the thing itself.
Related to memory through an old root meaning to be anxious or remember. Mourning is etymologically an act of remembering, not of sadness.
Shares a root with the German gern, gladly. The ache and the gladness are the same word underneath, which feels about right.

title: Gym Rat
blurb: Posted at 5:40am so you would know.

words.note: A deliberate misspelling of swollen, which is what it actually describes. Gym slang is unusually honest about mechanisms.
The countable plural is the giveaway — gains are treated as a possession you can lose, hence the fear of losing them.

words.definition: A cleanse with no medical meaning.
words.note: A real clinical term borrowed by the wellness industry. Your liver was already doing this, for free, the entire time.
From the Latin vigere, to be lively — the same root as vigil and vigilant. Staying awake and being strong were once the same idea.
One of the oldest words in English, cognate with the Sanskrit svedas. Humans have needed this word for as long as there have been words.

title: Old Words, New Energy
blurb: Medieval insults that deserve a comeback.

words.definition: To strike down, usually from above.
words.note: Also, bafflingly, to be smitten — struck by love. English decided being hit hard and falling in love warranted the same verb.

words.definition: A dishonest man of low standing.
words.note: Originally just meant boy, with no insult intended. It spent five hundred years sliding downhill, which is the usual fate of words for young men.
Meant a free peasant — a social rank, not a judgement. Churlish is what the upper classes decided that rank implied.

words.definition: A female fox. A woman with a temper.
words.note: One of the few English words preserving an old southern dialect habit of voicing an initial f into a v. Fixen became vixen and stuck.

words.definition: A likeable scoundrel; or something gone off-script.
words.note: Appeared suddenly in the 1560s with no clear ancestor. A word for people who go off on their own that itself came from nowhere.

title: Running on Empty
blurb: You are fine. You are definitely fine.

words.definition: Used up, with nothing held back.
words.note: The same word for money and for energy, which is not a metaphor English chose so much as one it never questioned.

words.definition: Damaged by too much heat, for too long.
words.note: Burnt and burned are both correct; British English tends to burnt for the adjective. Burnout borrowed the image wholesale in the 1970s.
Origin genuinely unknown — it simply appears in American English in the 1890s. Possibly a blend of woozle and boozy, possibly nothing.

words.definition: To sleep suddenly and without ceremony.
words.note: The sleep sense comes from 1960s counterculture — crash pad predates crashing out. It has always implied you did not plan it.

words.definition: What is left at the bottom.
words.note: From Old Norse dregg. One of the many words Vikings left in English, alongside sky, knife, and — fittingly — ransack.

title: Mise En Place
blurb: Everything in its place, before the shouting starts.

words.note: The tool is named after the action, not the other way round. The verb comes from an Old Norse word for a rapid sweeping movement, which is also why a train can whisk you somewhere.

words.definition: To work dough with your hands.
words.note: An Old English word, and a close relative of the German kneten. Unrelated to need, which is a much older and gloomier word that merely sounds the same.

words.definition: The fungus doing all the work.
words.note: The root means to boil or foam, which is what people could actually observe. Nobody knew yeast was alive until Pasteur, but the word had described its behaviour for a thousand years.

words.definition: To spoon the fat back over.
words.note: Confusingly, there is an unrelated baste meaning to sew loosely, and a third meaning to beat soundly. English kept all three and let context sort it out.

words.definition: A leaf you were told to like.
words.note: Short for Swiss chard, which is not Swiss. A Swiss botanist named it, and the label stuck to a Mediterranean plant that had never been near the Alps.

title: Dark By Four
blurb: Five words for the same grey month.

words.definition: Ice formed straight out of the air.
words.note: Shares a root with freeze, obviously, but also with the word for a hard crust. Frost is etymologically the skin the cold puts on things.
A Germanic word with cousins across northern Europe, which is roughly the distribution of people who have needed a specific word for this.

words.definition: Dim and hard to see through.
words.note: From an Old Norse word for darkness. It only picked up the sense of morally dubious in the nineteenth century, when murky dealings started appearing in print.

words.definition: Cold in a way you are supposed to enjoy.
words.note: Probably a reshaping of the French brusque. The same word gave English both brisk and brusque, which now describe a pleasant walk and an unpleasant person.
From balm, the soothing ointment. The mad sense is separate and probably from barmy, meaning frothy like beer barm, which English then confused with balmy and never untangled.

title: The Heist
blurb: It was going so well until the fourth word.

words.note: American underworld slang from the 1920s, almost certainly a pronunciation of hoist. To hoist goods was to steal them long before anyone pulled a heist.
Latin for elsewhere, and originally used in English exactly that literally. It only came to mean the excuse itself, rather than the fact, in the twentieth century.

words.definition: Someone convicted of a serious crime.
words.note: Also, still, a medical term for an infection at the fingertip. The two senses have coexisted for centuries with no one much bothered by it.
The same word for honest smithing and dishonest documents, both from the Latin fabricare, to fashion. The forger and the blacksmith are doing etymologically identical work.

words.definition: A crime with a sense of humour.
words.note: From the Italian capriola, a goat's leap — the same root as Capricorn. A caper is named for skipping about, which is why the word refuses to sound serious.

title: Four AM
blurb: You have checked the time twice now.

words.definition: What you would rather be doing.
words.note: The Old English dream meant joy, music, or revelry — not sleep at all. The modern sense probably arrived from Old Norse and quietly replaced it.
One of a family of words English built straight from the sound: snore, snort, sneeze, snarl, sniff. The initial sn- doing the work of a nose.
Began as a falconry term for a hawk shaking its feathers. It moved from birds to people to crowds, gathering force at every step.
From the Latin vigilia, a watch kept at night — the same root as vigour and vigilant. Staying awake, being strong and paying attention were once one idea.
Built from slow plus the -th that turns an adjective into a noun, exactly as warm becomes warmth. The animal was named after the sin, not the reverse.

title: In A Minor Key
blurb: Put it on and stare out of the window.

words.note: Italian for time, straight from the Latin tempus. Most of the vocabulary of Western music is Italian because Italy was where the notation was standardised.

words.definition: Notes agreeing to be heard together.
words.note: Shortened from accord, meaning agreement. The spelling with an h was borrowed later from cord, the string — so the word has two unrelated ancestors fused together.
From the Latin versus, a turning — specifically the turn of a plough at the end of a furrow. A line of poetry is named after where the writing turns back.

words.definition: To sing low and close to the microphone.
words.note: A Scots and northern English word for a low murmur, which was sitting unused until amplification made quiet singing possible in the 1920s.
From dirige, the first word of a Latin antiphon sung in the office for the dead. An entire genre named after the opening word of one hymn.

title: Down To The Wire
blurb: Payday is Friday. It is Tuesday.

words.note: British slang, a clipped form of skinned — as in skinned alive, or fleeced. The image is of having had everything taken off you.
Originally the past participle of break, used of a merchant whose business had broken. Bankrupt is the same idea in Italian: banca rotta, a broken bench.

words.definition: To squeeze. To economise. To steal.
words.note: All three senses are the same word narrowing and widening over six hundred years. Feeling the pinch and pinching something are cousins.
From Old Norse skamt, short. It is one of the few English adjectives that still sounds slightly wrong as a verb, though scanting was once perfectly ordinary.

words.definition: Thin in a way that worries people.
words.note: Origin genuinely uncertain — possibly from a Scandinavian word for a lean horse. One of those words that arrived in the 1400s without papers.

title: Unresolved Tension
blurb: Nobody has said anything yet.

words.definition: A feeling with no plan attached.
words.note: The romantic sense is American, from the 1880s, and the metaphor is physical: being crushed. English chose the most violent available verb for the least dangerous feeling.
First meant to flick or dart something away — you could flirt a fan open. The human sense came from the quick, glancing movement.

words.definition: To go weak in a satisfying way.
words.note: An Old English word meaning to faint, related to a root for suffocating. It survived mostly because Victorian novelists found it so useful.
Also an old English verb meaning to court someone — to go sparking. The romantic sense is a good deal older than anyone assumes.
The same word as a royal court, and that is the point: courting meant behaving as one did at court, with all its formality and audience.

title: Circle Back
blurb: Five words that mean nothing and never stop.

words.note: From the Latin quota pars, how great a part. It entered English as accounting vocabulary and has been used to apply pressure ever since.

words.definition: What a company believes it is.
words.note: Originally a burning piece of wood, then the mark burned into livestock to show ownership. Every brand is etymologically a scar proving who owns the animal.

words.definition: Admitting the plan was wrong, expensively.
words.note: A pivot is the fixed pin a thing turns on — so a company that pivots is claiming, flatteringly, that it has not moved at all.

words.definition: Customers leaving as fast as they arrive.
words.note: From the butter churn: violent repetitive motion that produces a result. Business borrowed the agitation and quietly dropped the part where you get butter.
Student slang for a hard worker by the 1800s, long before hustle culture. The sense of wearing something down by friction was always there.

title: Look Up
blurb: All five are further away than you think.

words.definition: A path that keeps falling and missing.
words.note: From the Latin orbita, a wheel track or rut. It also still means the bony socket of your eye, which is the older English sense.

words.definition: Ice on a very long loop.
words.note: From the Greek for long-haired — komētēs. The Greeks named it for the tail, describing it as a star wearing its hair loose.
The same root gives lunatic, from a genuine old belief that the moon's phases affected the mind. The medical term outlived the theory by centuries.
The solar plexus is named by the same logic as a comet's hair: the nerves radiate outward from the centre like drawn sunbeams.
Origin unknown, appearing in the 1500s meaning to spread outward. The light sense and the trouser sense are the same word doing the same job.

title: Seeing Red
blurb: You are not angry. You are just disappointed.

words.definition: Angry, and slightly formal about it.
words.note: From the Latin ira, anger — the same root as ire and irascible. It is the word newspapers use when they mean furious but want to sound neutral.

words.definition: Anger with the volume of a sermon.
words.note: Built from an Old English word meaning twisted or bent — the same root as writhe and wreath. Rage as something that contorts you.

words.definition: Wanting worse for someone, at your own cost.
words.note: A shortening of despite, which meant contempt. In spite of still carries the original sense: doing something in contempt of an obstacle.
An American variant of roiled, meaning to stir up sediment in water. To rile someone is to make them cloudy.

words.definition: Poison, or the tone of voice.
words.note: From the Latin venenum, which originally meant a potion or drug of any kind — including love potions, and shares a root with Venus.

title: Not Quite A Lie
blurb: Technically everything said here was true.

words.note: Also a steep headland, and the two are unrelated. The poker sense came from a Dutch word meaning to brag; the cliff is a separate nautical borrowing.

words.definition: To perform a feeling you do not have.
words.note: From the Latin fingere, to shape or mould — the same root as fiction and figment. Pretending and sculpting were once the same verb.
The garment is named after its shape: the Medieval Latin clocca meant a bell, and a hanging cloak looks like one. Clock comes from the same word.
From the same Germanic root as wise, as in likewise and in no wise — meaning manner or way. A guise is literally a way of appearing.
Nineteenth-century slang for counterfeit money, and that sense came first. A snide remark is etymologically a forged one.

title: Still In The Drawer
blurb: You are keeping these in case they come back.

words.definition: The sound of the internet arriving.
words.note: A portmanteau of modulator-demodulator, which is exactly what it does: turns data into noise a phone line can carry, then back again.

words.definition: It told you to find a phone.
words.note: From page, meaning to summon — as a hotel page boy once did by walking through the lobby calling a name. The device automated the boy.

words.definition: The format that refused to die.
words.note: Coined by chemists from the Latin vinum, wine, because the compound was first derived from ethanol. The word for records is named after wine.
Latin for backwards, and only used on its own as an adjective from the 1960s — which means the word retro is itself younger than most things called retro.
Tape is an Old English word for a narrow strip of cloth. It survived every change of technology because the shape never changed.

title: Out Of Signal
blurb: Nobody can reach either of you.

words.note: An Old English word with no known relatives in other languages — unusual for such a common word. It has meant the same thing for as long as English has existed.
Two unrelated words. To brook no argument comes from an Old English verb meaning to use or enjoy, which has nothing to do with water.
Among the oldest tree names in the language, traceable to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning bright — named for the bark, thousands of years ago.
Heathen comes from it: a heath-dweller, someone living out past the settlements where the new religion had not reached. An insult built out of a landscape.

words.definition: A clearing with light in it.
words.note: Probably related to glad, which originally meant bright or shining rather than happy. A glade is the bright patch in a dark wood.

title: One More Round
blurb: It is a school night and everyone knows it.

words.definition: Cold, and not asking much of you.
words.note: From the German Lagerbier, storehouse beer — it was brewed to be kept. The name describes the warehouse, not the drink.
Traces back through Latin and Greek to a Hebrew word, shekar, meaning strong drink. It arrived in English via the Bible before it meant apples specifically.

words.definition: Dark, and a meal in itself.
words.note: The beer is named after the adjective meaning strong or thickset. Stout ale simply meant strong ale, and the noun outlived the phrase.
Genuinely from toasted bread: spiced toast was dropped into wine to flavour it, and the person honoured was said to be the toast of the drink.
From the Latin sobrius, which appears to be se- (without) plus ebrius (drunk) — the same ebrius behind inebriated. Sober is literally un-drunk.

title: Something Moved
blurb: It was the house settling. Obviously.

words.definition: Fear that arrives all at once.
words.note: Named for the god Pan, who was believed to cause sudden groundless terror in lonely places. One of the few emotions named after a specific deity.
An Old English verb, and a Quaker was originally a mocking nickname — for people said to tremble at the word of the Lord. The group kept the insult.
From a Middle Low German word meaning to squat or crouch. Unrelated to coward, which comes from the Latin for tail, as in an animal turning tail.
The noun for an unpleasant person is American, from the 1880s. The plural the creeps — that crawling sensation — is older than the insult.

words.definition: Wrong in a way you cannot name.
words.note: Originally Scots and northern English, and it first meant fearful rather than frightening — you were eerie, the ghost was not. The word swapped ends.

title: House Always Wins
blurb: You are up. You should leave. You will not.

words.note: From an Old North French word related to gage, a pledge — the same root as engage and mortgage. A wager was originally the security, not the bet.
Probably from the literal stake — a post driven into the ground, on which the prize was placed for all to see. The money sat on a stick in the middle.
Casinos use tokens precisely because chips do not feel like money. The word is just the ordinary chip, a small fragment, doing psychological work.
Luck came into English from Dutch or Low German, and it arrived through gambling — the earliest English uses are all about games of chance.
From nineteenth-century billiards, for an accidentally successful shot. There are also fluke the flatfish and fluke the parasite, all three unrelated.

title: Last Word
blurb: Five ways to keep talking.

words.note: From the Latin quotare, to number — medieval scribes quoted a text by marking it with numbers to reference it. The sense of repeating came later.
Probably a frequentative of draw, as in drawing the words out. English builds a lot of verbs this way: sparkle from spark, crackle from crack.
Origin uncertain, in English since the 1200s. It once meant a threat as much as a brag, which tells you something about how boasting was received.
Possibly from the French tant pour tant, tit for tat — a taunt as a reply given in kind. Fittingly, the word for a comeback may itself be a comeback.
From an Old French word meaning to thrust back, built on but, an end or blow — the same root as butt. A rebuttal is a headbutt with sources.

title: Worn In
blurb: You have had all of these too long.

words.definition: The most successful fabric ever made.
words.note: From serge de Nîmes, the French town. Jeans are named after Genoa by the same logic, so a pair of denim jeans is named after two cities at once.
Arrived in English from Persian via Urdu, along with the garment itself, in the eighteenth century. One of many textile words English imported wholesale.

words.definition: Cloth for pretending to like walking.
words.note: Almost certainly a misreading. A clerk wrote tweel — Scots for twill — and someone read it as tweed, thinking of the river. The error became the name.
From the Latin laqueus, a noose or snare, via French. Delicate lace and the lace in your shoe are the same word, both named after a loop that catches.
Originally a monk's habit, which is why a disgraced priest is defrocked. The word travelled from monastery to wardrobe and kept only one foot in each.

title: Under The Skin
blurb: All present and doing their jobs.

words.note: From the Latin pulsus, a beating — the same root as impulse and repel. There is also pulse the lentil, entirely unrelated, from a word for porridge.
The Latin spina meant a thorn. The backbone is named after its spiky projections, which is also why a hedgehog's spines and your spine are one word.
The Latin nervus meant sinew or bowstring — the Greeks and Romans did not distinguish nerves from tendons. The confusion is preserved in the word.
From the Latin mola, a millstone. Named for the job rather than the shape, by people who ground their own flour and saw the resemblance daily.
From the Latin lympha, clear spring water — which was itself probably an alteration of nympha, the water spirit. A body fluid named after a nymph.

title: Running Late
blurb: You said you had left twenty minutes ago.

words.definition: A stretch of time with a character.
words.note: From a Greek word meaning a stopping point — the fixed moment from which time is measured, not the span itself. The modern sense inverts the original.

words.definition: The thing you are losing to.
words.note: From the Medieval Latin clocca, a bell, because early public clocks marked hours by ringing rather than by a face. Cloak comes from the same word.
Haste arrived from Old French but goes back to a Germanic root meaning violence or force. Hurrying was originally an act of aggression.
From the Latin tardus, slow — the same root as retard in its original neutral sense of delay. It is the word institutions use when they mean late.
From Old French delaier, built on the Latin dilatare, to spread out or widen. A delay is etymologically time being stretched rather than lost.
